title: Swapping bands between the two clubs and the Riviera's decline
summary: The owners swap Eckstine's band for Pillars's, and cheaper acts and weaker business lead the Riviera to close in 1945.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So after he was there a week, they made a deal with Mr. Jordan George and Chambers, to bring our band back.

To bring our band back to the Plantation, and take his band over to the Club Riviera. And, of course, Billy Eckstine was a big hit over there, because he had just left Earl Hines not too long before that, where he had sung that "you know?" song Jelly Jelly, you know? And so it was mutually agreed that the two nightclub owners would do that, see. So we went back and played the two weeks out, you know. Then we came on back to the Club Riviera, and I just forget who followed us in there, but they started bringing in big names. Cab came in there, and I mentioned that before. I'm trying to think of some other acts.

They drew big crowds for a while, but by late summer, they had died down. So they tried to go in for cheaper acts, see. And they just didn't get it. And business just started dying down. And in the following year, 1945, they went out of business. Went out of business.
